claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure in its as-synthesized state.
The proposed surrogate will combine multiscale electron-microscopy data with high-resolution microstructural descriptors.
The proposed surrogate will be trained using partial mechanical-test results.
A machine-learning surrogate using microstructure-sensitive descriptors can predict Young's modulus for HfNbTiVAl10.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict the yield strength of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile loading.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict fracture-related behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
The model will predict the stated mechanical responses approximately ten times faster than established continuum or ab initio simulations.
The model will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to established continuum or ab initio simulations.
The proposed tests will span room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
Testing at varied strain rates and temperatures will capture both elastic and inelastic deformation regimes.
The relevant structural descriptors include precipitate distributions, phase boundaries, and localized defect concentrations.
Learning correlations between fine-scale hierarchical descriptors and macroscopic responses can improve prediction fidelity.
Use of the learned surrogate will reduce computational expense relative to conventional simulations.
Conventional continuum and ab initio models are computationally intensive.
Conventional continuum and ab initio models are less able to capture HfNbTiVAl10's multiscale heterogeneity.
The surrogate may fail if imaging-derived descriptors omit mechanically important hierarchical features.
The surrogate may fail if its training data do not represent process-induced microstructural variations.
Independent validation will falsify the hypothesis if prediction error is not reduced by at least 15–20% or prediction time is not at least 5–10 times faster than the simulation baseline.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis claims an order-of-magnitude, approximately 10× speedup, whereas the falsification rule permits a result as low as 5× to avoid falsification. Thus the declared test does not decisively test the headline speed claim.
